newsitem.title: USA: IRS Southeast region probing tax-exempt bond deals.
newsitem.headline: IRS Southeast region probing tax-exempt bond deals.

text.p: The IRS' Southeast office is probing a stunning number of tax-exempt bond deals in its 14-state jurisdiction for possible tax-law violations, including seven separate "yield burning" probes, an IRS manager said on Friday.

"We've managed to stumble upon (a lot of) things out there. It's quite astounding the number of cases we have going. It's incredulous to me," said Charles Anderson, who oversees a team of Internal Revenue Service agents in the Service's Baltimore complex who have been monitoring Southeastern U.S. tax-exempt bond deals for a year.
Anderson spoke on a panel on IRS enforcement issues in the municipal bond market at the National Association of Bond Lawyers' Washington seminar here.
Anderson said his team has issued about 30 letters to bond issuers announcing a "preliminary" IRS finding that their bonds have been deemed taxable.

"I would anticipate in the next five to six months that we may have another 40 to 50. So we are talking eventually 80 closing agreement discussions in one region," he said. "That was the surprising part - finding as much stuff this quickly," he added.

Anderson said he is "surprised" that of the 30 deals found taxable by his region so far, only three were "disclosed publicly." He said that his region is going to "insist" that conduit borrowers publicize the fact when they sign closing agreements with IRS.
In other cases, Anderson said his region has a "whole bunch" of "pure arbitrage" matters.

"The bonds are sold, people take money out, they buy a guaranteed investment contract (GIC) at higher rates, the money's never spent and the GIC redeems the bonds at the end," Anderson said. "We have several dozen of these."

Anderson said his region has seven yield burning probes in the works. Yield burning refers to allegations that bond underwriters overcharge states and localities for U.S. Treasury securities they bought to help them refinance outstanding bonds.
He said in some of the cases, the "providers of the securities were getting paid by the underwriters."
This is a "wake up" call to bond issuers, Anderson said. Issuers "ought to be asking" questions of firms handling their refinancings, he said.

"I think this is a real big problem in just the cases I've seen," Anderson said. "It is staggering to me that this is out there. This is like the goose that laid the golden egg," said Anderson, referring to possible returns to the IRS from any closing agreements the Service reaches with issuers.

"I think yield burning is an example of how the government can lose a lot of money that could be used in other areas," said Anderson, who stressed his views were his own and not necessarily those of the IRS. He noted that the director of his IRS region is "not very happy" about issuers being hit with the bill for yield burning "when others have profited."
He was referring to a controversial closing agreement plan announced by IRS last year. The plan, spelled out in IRS revenue procedure 96-41, "is just an option," he said.
Turning to IRS's new random audit program, which is examining 100 small issue industrial development bonds nationwide, Anderson said his region is "catching a lot of fish."

"I have a number of them that I'm pretty confident that we will reach adverse positions (in)," he said. The staff is seeing a lot of "big Fortune 500 companies" who have a "bunch of these small issues out there," Anderson said.
Overall, said Anderson, his region "wants to work actively toward resolving (pending cases) in ways that protect bondholders and issuers."

"(But) I won't lose any sleep about taxing a bondholder if the issuer is at fault," he said. "I am (however) sympathetic for where we can work out closing agreements with others who have malpractice insurance, even if it involves holding off until lawsuits go through the system. We want to work toward a more flexible way of resolving cases."
